extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent litigators, judges, and law students studying patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on affirmative and other defenses available to a defendant in a patent-infringement action (statutes of limitation, estoppel, release, res adjudicata, and constraints on defenses such as estoppel and licensee rules). Explains when each defense applies and important exceptions and procedural timing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutes of Limitation (timing for infringement suits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suit for infringement must be brought within the time limits prescribed by applicable statutes (federal and/or state); where a patent term is extended or repealed statutes may affect accrual and available recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal statute: actions are limited to six years after expiration of the patent/extended term; if suit is brought within five years after expiration of an extended term plaintiff may recover only for infringements during the extension. Statutes of limitation are generally prospective and do not revive already-barred rights; repeal of a federal limitation clause may not relieve previously existing limits. Where the federal statute is inapplicable (e.g., infringement occurred after repeal) state limitation statutes may govern. Because of historical repeals and jurisdictional uncertainty, limitations defences require careful, case-specific analysis. (Illustrative authorities cited: Sayles v. Dubuque & Sioux City R. R. Co.; Vaughn v. East Tennessee, Virginia, & Georgia R. R. Co.; May v. Logan Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel (estoppel in pais and related doctrines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel as a defence alleges that plaintiff's conduct (acts, omissions, or relations) has reasonably misled the defendant so that plaintiff should be barred from pursuing the remedy. Both equitable and legal forms are recognized, with equitable estoppel sometimes broader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core principles: estoppel arises when plaintiff intentionally or negligently misleads defendant, or when plaintiff omitted duties whose performance would have prevented defendant's actions. Equity focuses on effect of conduct, not motive; courts of law have increasingly adopted wider equitable views. Specific applications and limits: (1) Silence works as estoppel only where there was a duty to speak. (2) Failure to mark patented articles ('patented' stamping) estops patentee from claiming substantial damages for infringements occurring before the defendant received notice. (3) Delay in suing may create estoppel in equity (laches) but is less certain at law unless it evidences abandonment. (4) A suit against one infringer gives notice to others; subsequent delay cannot create estoppel as to them. (5) Actions creating an implied license (e.g., extensive tolerated use) may be treated as estoppel. (6) Relations such as transferor/transferee or prior ownership can create estoppel — e.g., a former owner in a suit by his assignee cannot deny validity. (7) Limitations: mere fact defendant was misled is not always sufficient; the conduct must be such that plaintiff should reasonably have expected the defendant to be influenced. Examples and authorities are given (Pickard v. Sears; Bassett v. Bradley; Greenwood v. Bracher; Gear v. Grosvenor; others). Also noted: estoppel may bar recovery of damages but may not always bar injunctive relief depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release (surrender or release bars the cause of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff's voluntary surrender of the patent to the government or a release to an alleged infringer extinguishes the cause of action; a valid release is a complete defence to an infringement suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two methods: (1) surrender of the patent to the government terminates patent and all rights of action; (2) a release to the infringer terminates the cause of action but not the patent. Releases may be written (under seal) or implied from circumstances. Requirements and limits: releasor must have legal right to grant the release; release must be in good faith and not in fraud of co-owners; conditional releases are effective only if conditions are fulfilled; a release taken with notice is subject to equities of other owners. A valid release operates both as contract relinquishing the cause and as an estoppel preventing subsequent pursuit. (Authorities and illustrative cases cited: Goodyear v. McBamey; Babcock & Wilcox Co. v. Pioneer Iron Works; see also §787, 789 references.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Res adjudicata (prior final judgment as a bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: A final judgment on the merits that adjudicated the same issue between the same parties is a defence to a later suit for the same infringement or issue; recovery merges the tort into contract where appropriate and satisfaction of judgment destroys the cause of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements: prior judgment must be final, on the merits, and cover the same issue of infringement or title. Effects and limits: a judgment for defendant is conclusive and estops the plaintiff as to matters litigated and decided; interlocutory decisions, consent decrees in collateral proceedings, or suits dismissed for want of prosecution generally do not constitute res adjudicata. A prior recovery by plaintiff against defendant ordinarily bars a second suit on the same act; judgment between patentees on priority can affect title of junior patentee but may not bar other distinct claims. State court judgments are not always conclusive on title in federal courts. Special rules apply for joint infringers and licensees. (Authorities and examples cited: Lyon v. Perin & Gaff Mfg. Co.; United States Metallic Packing Co. v. Tripp; Steam Gauge & Lantern Co. v. Meyrose; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant may plead any defence unless estopped (limitations on availability of defences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant is entitled to set up any of the recognized defences in an infringement suit unless he is estopped from doing so by his own prior conduct or agreements; prior conduct binds defendants as it does plaintiffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule: all defenses enumerated may be pleaded unless defendant's prior acts, admissions, licenses, or transactions estop him. Illustrative constraints: (1) A licensee cannot attack the validity of the patent while the license is in force (except to show the license was exceeded); to challenge validity the licensee must repudiate the license. (2) A former owner or assignor through whom plaintiff's title derives generally cannot deny validity. (3) A defendant who has used and advertised an invention may be estopped from claiming it lacks utility. (4) Fraudulent patentees who knowingly procured invalid patents may be estopped from asserting certain defences; conversely bona fide patentees defeated in interference may sometimes later challenge patentability. (5) Prior positions (e.g., letting another take out a patent, accepting license fees, etc.) can preclude inconsistent defenses. Parties must examine whether prior litigation positions, transfers, covenants (e.g., covenants not to contest validity), or conduct create estoppel before pleading certain defences. (Authorities and many case examples cited throughout.)
